title: Memory Systems Detective
summary: Judge five claims about separable memory systems against five fictional memory profiles. For each pairing, decide whether the profile supports the claim, counts against it, or cannot decide it.
learningObjectives: State what a profile must contain before it supports a distinction between memory systems.
Distinguish the claim that two tasks are separable from the claim that two systems exist.
Explain why normal recognition with impaired recall does not establish a retrieval account.
Identify task impurity in a profile where every impaired measure shares its material.
List the non-neurological explanations of a uniformly slightly-below-average profile.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native radio and button controls throughout. The profile chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving every measure, what it asks the person to do, the distance from its own control group and its standing in words. Every bar also prints its own value, so the fill is redundant, and bars clearly outside the control range are distinguished by fill and by a wording in the table rather than by colour alone. The claim under judgement sits in a goal banner in the interactive header, so it is readable while the verdict radios at the bottom of the control column are used, and the profile chart is pinned at 294px so the evidence stays on screen. Grid cells print the verdict as a word and add the intended verdict when they differ. Every judgement announces through the shell's polite live region with a running count. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: When a memory profile supports a distinction between systems, when it counts against one, and the twelve times out of twenty-five that it cannot decide
simulationNotes: Five invented profiles with invented numbers on seven invented measures, each expressed as a distance from the average of that measure's own fictional control group in control standard deviations. A measure counts as clearly below its controls at minus two or lower and as within range above about minus 1.2. The intended grid, rows being the five claims and columns profiles A to E: short-term against episodic gives support, support, support, cannot, cannot; episodic against semantic gives support, cannot, support, cannot, cannot; episodic against skill gives support, cannot, support, cannot, cannot; retrieval against storage gives cannot in all five; and one general reduction gives against, against, against, against, support. Eight cells support a claim, five count against one, and twelve cannot decide. The retrieval row is never supported anywhere, deliberately: the pattern always cited for it - recall at floor with normal recognition - does not establish it, because recognition is the easier task and a trace too weak to be recalled can still be strong enough to be recognised. Deliberate simplifications: seven measures is very few, real batteries separate several things merged here, and the intended answers are judgements the tool invites the learner to argue with. No anatomy appears anywhere, because these distinctions are between what tasks require. No real person, published case, clinical instrument or syndrome name is used, and nothing on the page diagnoses anybody or offers a prognosis.
